text:
Lots of great updates on the site in the past couple days as I've been working through all of the gaps we've had over the years. Generally the big work has been done, but we just need to iron out the details (as with BE and DLL builds). Getting rid of Boost, and the other dependencies over time, made all of it a LOT easier.

`Big Endian` (s390x), Windows `DLL builds`, `CMake for Windows` (with presets), `clang-cl` (native VS/Windows open source compiler), `MinGW-w64 GCC`, `MinGW-w64 Clang`, `arm32`, `clang-cl arm64`... literally every combination of mac/win/linux on any hardware, any major compiler or build system, with nearly every hardware optimization, all verified in CI - using cross-compile and in a few cases emulators for test execution.

AND

`deterministic builds`, tested in pairs, executed in `Guix` (verifiable build chain) using all of the libbitcoin-build code generation machinery, running in GH actions in Phillip's new release flow.

AND

`packaging` for `apt (deb)` (Linux), `Homebrew` (macOS), `winget` (windows), `Docker` (github), `Umbrel` and `StartOS` (bitcoin), also running in GH actions, pulling signed binaries from the release outputs - and soon automated submission.

AND

`bx` not far behind for the full monte.

text:
I've changed `bip90` to off by default. It's the only hard fork we've been carrying, and there's no reason for it. It costs 10-15 seconds on the header sync to disable it. It's a hard fork material query optimization for Core, but we don't need it.

I pointed out that it was a hard fork when they documented it, and they argued about it, called it a hard fork, and then reverted that status to unspecified. And after that they never documented another, but there have been `seven others` by my count (4 hard forks, 3 soft forks). The only difference with bip90 is that they posted it to a website after the fact.

That's not counting the LevelDB bug, stopgap, and removal, or the inflation bug and removal. That's 5 more forks (3 hard, 2 soft), but since those weren't intentional, I'm discounting them above.

elements.text: Turns out there was an integer version of the std::stream-based number parser in use in several places in the client-server interfaces, and it has the same flaw. every thread passed thru a critical section. Also the json parser had a dumb perf flaw. And the http serializer was sending header and body independently. With that and one io scheduler optimization, the perf is back to pre-boost-removal baseline, with significant improvement in many regions (almost 2x in some case). Also building with the verbose logging level disabled increase http server performance at every level by about 10%.

With that and one io scheduler optimization, the perf is back to pre-boost-removal baseline, with significant improvement in many regions (almost 2x in some case). Also building with the verbose logging level disabled increase http server performance at every level by about 10%.
